title: Build your own per-letter lowercase table and Greek "ΟΔΥΣΣΕΥΣ" lowercases to the wrong letter at the end
assumption: Lowercasing a string is just mapping each character to its lowercase equivalent, independent of its neighbors.

input.description: A hand-rolled case-folding table (common in custom search normalizers, or a simple transliteration helper) that maps each character independently, rather than calling the language's real lowercasing routine.

what_goes_wrong: A search-index normalizer built this way produces a lowercase form that disagrees with the one str.lower() / toLowerCase() produces, so a lookup built against one and compared against the other silently fails to match at the end of every Greek word ending in capital sigma.
why: Greek has two lowercase forms of sigma: σ in the middle of a word and ς (final sigma) at the end of a word — which form is correct depends on the character's POSITION in the word, not just its identity. Unicode's SpecialCasing rules encode that context-sensitive mapping, and both Python's str.lower() and JavaScript's toLowerCase() correctly apply it. A naive table that maps Σ to σ unconditionally, character by character with no notion of 'end of word', can never produce the final form, so it disagrees with the correct, built-in result precisely where a word ends in sigma.
affects: any hand-rolled per-character case table (no word-context)
fix: Never build a custom per-character case-folding table for a script you haven't checked for context-sensitive rules; use the language's built-in Unicode-aware lower()/toLowerCase() (or ICU) and only post-process it if you have a specific, tested reason to.

test_cases.note: If you built your own per-character lowercase table, verify it against this: the correct result ends in final sigma (ς), not plain sigma (σ).
